q: Which of these is shared by all threads of the same process?
a: Heap and global data (the address space)
e: Each thread has its own stack, PC and registers. Code, heap, globals and open files are shared.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
e: The condition is NO preemption. If resources can be preempted, deadlock cannot happen.

q: The Banker's algorithm is used for:
e: It grants a request only if the system stays in a safe state, which is avoidance. Prevention breaks one of the four conditions.

q: Four processes all arrive at time 0 with burst times 6, 8, 7, 3. What is the average waiting time under non-preemptive SJF?
e: The order is 3, 6, 7, 8, so the waits are 0, 3, 9, 16 and the average is 28/4 = 7. FCFS would give 10.25.

q: Belady's anomaly (more frames causing MORE page faults) can happen with:
e: LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms and never show Belady's anomaly. FIFO can.

q: Reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 with 3 frames under LRU. How many page faults?
e: Faults on 7, 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4. The two later 0s are hits.

q: Thrashing means:
a: The system spends more time swapping pages than doing useful work
w: The CPU is idle because no process is ready
Two processes wait for each other forever
A process uses up its time slice too often
e: It is caused by too little memory for the working sets. Fix it by lowering the degree of multiprogramming or by using a working-set model.

q: The main difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore is:
a: A mutex has ownership: only the thread that locked it should unlock it
w: A semaphore can only take the values 0 and 1
A mutex can be used for signalling between processes but a semaphore cannot
e: Semaphores are signalling tools that any thread can post. A mutex is a lock owned by one thread.

q: 32-bit virtual addresses, 4 KB pages. How many entries are in a single-level page table?
e: 4 KB = 2^12, so the offset uses 12 bits. That leaves 20 bits for the page number, so 2^20 entries.

q: Why is a context switch between threads of the same process cheaper than between processes?
a: The address space stays the same, so there is no page-table switch or TLB flush
e: The thread switch still saves and restores registers and the stack pointer, but the memory mapping does not change.

q: Round Robin with a very large time quantum behaves like:
e: If no process ever uses up its quantum, processes simply run in arrival order.

q: Starvation in priority scheduling is usually fixed with:
e: Aging slowly raises the priority of processes that have waited a long time.

q: Paging can suffer from which kind of fragmentation?
e: The last page of a process may be partly empty (internal). Paging removes external fragmentation. Segmentation suffers from external fragmentation.

q: A zombie process is a process that:
a: Has finished, but its parent has not yet called wait() to read its exit status
w: Is still running after its parent has died
e: A running child whose parent has died is an orphan, and init/systemd adopts it.

q: A program calls fork() three times in a row and then prints "hi" once. How many times is "hi" printed?
e: Each fork doubles the number of processes: 2^3 = 8.

q: Which of these is NOT a requirement for a correct critical-section solution?
a: The shortest process must enter first
e: The three requirements are mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

q: The TCP three-way handshake is:
e: FIN is used to close the connection, which takes a four-way exchange.

q: DNS queries normally use:
e: DNS falls back to TCP for large responses and zone transfers.

q: A router mainly works at which OSI layer?
e: Routers forward packets by IP address. Switches forward frames by MAC address (Layer 2).

q: Which protocol is connectionless?
e: UDP has no handshake, no guaranteed delivery and no ordering. It is used for DNS, video calls and games.

q: Which HTTP status code means "you are identified, but you are not allowed to do this"?
e: 401 means you are not authenticated or your credentials are bad. 403 means you are authenticated but not permitted.

q: How many usable host addresses are there in a /26 IPv4 subnet?
e: 2^(32−26) = 64. Subtract the network and broadcast addresses to get 62.

q: Which protocol finds the MAC address for a known IPv4 address?
e: DHCP assigns IP addresses, DNS turns names into IPs, and ICMP is used by ping and traceroute.

q: Which HTTP method is idempotent?
e: Sending the same PUT again leaves the resource in the same state. POST may create duplicates. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent.

q: TCP flow control is done with:
e: Flow control protects the receiver. Congestion control (slow start, cwnd) protects the network.

q: Which address is a private IPv4 address?
In the OSI model, which layer is traditionally responsible for encryption and data formatting?
e: Session manages dialogues between applications. In TCP/IP, both are merged into the application layer.

q: How many bits long is an IPv6 address?
e: IPv4 is 32 bits and IPv6 is 128 bits.

q: "Each request carries everything the server needs, and the server stores no client session" describes which REST principle?
e: Statelessness makes horizontal scaling easy, because any server can handle any request.

q: During a TLS handshake, the shared symmetric session key is set up using:
a: An asymmetric key exchange such as (EC)DHE
e: Asymmetric cryptography sets up the key. Symmetric cryptography (such as AES) then encrypts the bulk data, because it is fast.

q: What does a switch use to forward frames?
e: A hub repeats each frame to all ports. A switch learns MAC addresses and sends frames only to the right port.

q: In ACID, "Isolation" means:
a: Concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate, uncommitted effects
w: A transaction runs completely or not at all
e: The wrong options describe Durability, Atomicity and Consistency.

q: Third Normal Form (3NF) mainly removes:
a: Transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on the key
w: Partial dependencies on part of a composite key
e: 1NF removes repeating groups, 2NF removes partial dependencies, 3NF removes transitive dependencies, and 4NF removes multivalued dependencies.

q: A relation is in BCNF if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y:
w: X is a primary key column
e: 3NF also allows Y to be prime. BCNF does not, so it is stricter.

q: Which join returns every row of the left table, with NULLs where there is no match?
e: INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows.

q: Table A has 3 rows and table B has 4 rows. How many rows does A CROSS JOIN B return?
e: A cross join is the Cartesian product: 3 × 4.

q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
a: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
w: WHERE can use aggregate functions such as COUNT()
e: You cannot write WHERE COUNT(*) > 5. Use HAVING for that.

q: Which command removes the table's data AND its structure?
e: DELETE removes rows (optionally with WHERE, and can be rolled back). TRUNCATE quickly removes all rows but keeps the table.

q: Adding an index to a column usually:
a: Makes reads/lookups faster but makes inserts and updates slower
w: Makes reads slower and writes faster
e: The index (often a B+ tree) must be updated on every write.

q: A primary key column must be:
e: A foreign key can contain duplicates and, unless it is constrained, NULLs.

q: A "dirty read" is:
a: Reading data written by another transaction that has not committed yet
w: Reading a row twice and getting different values
New rows appearing when a range query is repeated
e: Dirty reads are prevented from READ COMMITTED upwards. The wrong options describe a non-repeatable read and a phantom read.

q: Which query returns the second-highest salary?
a: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);
w: SELECT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary LIMIT 2;
e: Another way is ORDER BY salary DESC with LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 on DISTINCT salaries.

q: COUNT(column) differs from COUNT(*) because:
a: COUNT(column) ignores NULL values in that column
e: COUNT(DISTINCT column) is the one that counts distinct values.

q: How many clustered indexes can a table have?
e: A clustered index sets the physical order of the rows, and rows can only be stored in one order.

q: Runtime polymorphism is achieved through:
e: Overloading is resolved at compile time. Overriding is chosen at runtime through the vtable.

q: When is method overloading resolved?
e: The compiler picks the overload from the argument types.

q: In Java, what can an abstract class have that an interface cannot?
e: Since Java 8, interfaces can have default and static methods, but they still cannot have instance state or constructors.

q: Encapsulation is best described as:
a: Bundling data with the methods that use it, and restricting direct access to that data
w: Inheriting behaviour from a parent class
Hiding implementation behind an interface for multiple types
Creating many objects from one class
e: Abstraction is about showing only what is essential. Encapsulation is about protecting internal state.

q: In C++, the "diamond problem" of multiple inheritance is solved with:
e: With class B : virtual public A and class C : virtual public A, class D gets only one shared A subobject.

q: "A class should have only one reason to change" is which SOLID principle?
e: S = Single responsibility, O = Open/closed, L = Liskov, I = Interface segregation, D = Dependency inversion.

q: The Liskov Substitution Principle says:
a: Objects of a subclass should be usable wherever the base class is expected, without breaking correctness
w: A class should depend on abstractions
Classes should be open for extension
Clients should not depend on methods they don't use
e: The classic violation is Square extends Rectangle, where setting the width changes the height.

q: The Singleton pattern makes sure that:
a: A class has only one instance, with a global access point
w: Objects are created only through subclasses
e: In multithreaded code, the instance must be created in a thread-safe way.

q: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort?
e: It happens when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, for example a sorted array with the first element as pivot. The average is O(n log n).

q: Which sorting algorithm is stable?
e: Stable means equal keys keep their original order. Insertion sort and bubble sort are also stable.

q: Hash table lookup takes on average and in the worst case:
a: O(1) on average, O(n) in the worst case
e: The worst case happens when every key collides into the same bucket.

q: Which data structure does BFS use?
e: DFS uses a stack (or recursion). Dijkstra uses a priority queue.

q: An inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys:
e: This is the standard way to check whether a tree is a valid BST.

q: Dijkstra's algorithm may give wrong answers when the graph has:
e: Use Bellman-Ford when there are negative edges. Bellman-Ford can also detect negative cycles.

q: What does T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n solve to?
e: This is case 2 of the Master theorem, and it is the merge sort recurrence.

q: Building a binary heap from n unsorted elements with bottom-up heapify takes:
e: Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a short distance, so the total work is linear.

q: What is the minimum number of edges in a connected undirected graph with n vertices?
e: Such a graph is a tree. Adding one more edge creates a cycle.

q: for (i = 1..n) { for (j = 1; j < n; j *= 2) {...} } has complexity:
e: The inner loop doubles j each time, so it runs log n times for each of the n outer iterations.

q: What does the postfix expression 2 3 4 * + evaluate to?
e: Use a stack: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.

q: Which combination gives an LRU cache with O(1) get and put?
e: The map finds the node in O(1). The list moves the node to the front, or removes the oldest from the back, in O(1).

q: How many structurally different BSTs can be built from 3 distinct keys?
e: This is the Catalan number C3 = 5.

q: Which data structure is best for autocomplete (prefix search)?
e: Searching a prefix of length L takes O(L), and all words with that prefix are below that node.

q: Which algorithm detects a cycle in a DIRECTED graph?
a: DFS that tracks nodes on the current recursion stack (or Kahn's algorithm failing to process all nodes)
w: Plain BFS with a visited set
e: Union-Find works for undirected graphs but not directed ones. A visited node reached again in BFS is not always a cycle in a directed graph.

q: You need the minimum capacity that lets a task finish within D days, and the check "does capacity X work?" is monotonic. Which technique fits best?
e: Search over the range of possible answers. Each check is usually an O(n) greedy pass.

q: What is the height of a complete binary tree with n nodes?
e: Each level doubles the number of nodes, so the height is logarithmic.

q: Which is an example of SaaS?
e: IaaS gives you VMs (EC2). PaaS gives you a platform to deploy code (App Engine, Heroku). SaaS is finished software.

q: The key difference between containers and virtual machines is:
a: Containers share the host OS kernel. VMs each run a full guest OS on a hypervisor.
e: Because they share the kernel, containers are lighter and start faster, but they are less isolated.

q: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
e: A pod holds one or more containers that share network and storage. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets of pods.

q: Horizontal scaling means:
w: Adding more CPU/RAM to one machine
e: Vertical scaling (scale up) means making one machine bigger.

q: How are serverless functions (such as AWS Lambda) usually billed?
w: A fixed monthly price per server
e: Serverless functions scale to zero when idle. The trade-offs are cold starts and execution time limits.

q: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between:
e: Partitions cannot be avoided, so the real choice is between CP and AP.

q: Continuous Integration (CI) means:
a: Developers merge often, and every merge is automatically built and tested
w: Code is deployed to production by hand once a month
Only the QA team runs tests
e: Continuous Delivery and Deployment extend CI by automatically releasing the build.

q: Which AWS service is object storage?
e: In Azure this is Blob Storage, and in GCP it is Cloud Storage. RDS is managed relational databases.

q: Deploying across multiple Availability Zones mainly improves:
w: Per-request latency within a single zone
e: If one data centre fails, the others keep serving traffic.

q: Under the cloud shared-responsibility model, for IaaS the CUSTOMER is responsible for:
a: Their data, IAM permissions, OS patching and application security
w: The physical security of data centres
e: The provider secures the cloud itself. The customer secures what they put in it.

q: A CDN reduces latency mainly by:
a: Caching content on edge servers close to users
e: Examples include CloudFront, Akamai and Cloudflare.

q: In Docker, the relationship between an image and a container is:
a: A container is a running instance of an image
w: An image is a running container
e: A Dockerfile builds an image, an image is run as a container, and the same image can run as many containers.

q: A load balancer is mainly used to:
a: Spread incoming traffic across several servers
e: It also runs health checks and removes unhealthy instances from rotation.

q: Which of these is a symmetric encryption algorithm?
e: RSA and ECC are asymmetric. Diffie-Hellman is a key-exchange protocol.

q: How does hashing differ from encryption?
a: Hashing is one-way. Encryption can be reversed with a key.
w: Hashing needs a key to reverse
e: Hashes are used for integrity checks and storing passwords. Encryption is used for confidentiality.

q: What is the best way to store user passwords?
a: A salted, slow hash such as bcrypt or Argon2
w: Plain text in a protected table
AES encryption with a key stored in the code
e: The salt defeats rainbow tables, and the slow hash makes brute force expensive.

q: What is the most effective defence against SQL injection?
e: With parameters, user input is treated as data and never as SQL code.

q: To create a digital signature, the sender signs with:
e: Anyone can verify the signature with the sender's public key. This gives authenticity and non-repudiation.

q: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is:
a: Injecting malicious scripts into pages that other users view
w: Forging requests from a logged-in user's browser
e: The first wrong option describes CSRF and the second describes DoS. Defend against XSS with output encoding and a Content Security Policy.

q: How does React's virtual DOM improve performance?
a: It compares the new virtual tree with the old one and applies only the minimum changes to the real DOM
w: It replaces the browser's DOM completely
It runs JavaScript on the server only
e: This comparison step is called reconciliation.

q: In React, when does useEffect(fn, []) run fn (outside StrictMode development)?
a: Once, after the first render (on mount)
e: With no dependency array, it runs after every render. With [x], it runs whenever x changes.

q: A model with 99% training accuracy and 70% test accuracy is most likely:
e: Remedies include more data, regularisation, dropout, early stopping and simpler models.

q: Precision is defined as:
e: TP / (TP + FN) is recall. Precision asks how many of the predicted positives are correct. Recall asks how many of the real positives were found.

q: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mainly helps an LLM by:
a: Grounding its answers in relevant documents retrieved at query time
w: Training the model from scratch on company data
e: RAG lowers hallucination on company-specific questions without retraining the model. This is a common GenAI consulting use case.

q: Which is an example of supervised learning?
a: Classifying emails as spam using emails that already have labels
w: Grouping customers into segments without labels
An agent learning by trial and error from rewards
e: The wrong options are clustering (unsupervised), dimensionality reduction (unsupervised) and reinforcement learning.

q: The main advantage of microservices over a monolith is:
a: Each service can be deployed and scaled on its own
w: Simpler debugging and no network calls
e: The trade-offs are more complex operations, network latency and distributed data consistency.

q: Agile/Scrum delivers software:
a: Iteratively, in short sprints, with regular feedback
w: In one big release at the end
Only after all requirements are fixed up front
e: Delivering only after all requirements are fixed up front describes the Waterfall model.

q: What does `git rebase` do that `git merge` does not?
a: It rewrites history by replaying commits on top of another base
e: Never rebase commits that other people have already pulled. Use merge on shared branches.

q: An LLM "hallucination" is:
a: Fluent, confident output that is factually wrong or made up
e: Ways to reduce it include RAG, citations, lower temperature, human review and evaluation sets.
